The Mashona mole-rat (Fukomys darlingi) is a small, social bathyergid rodent inhabiting the mesic woodlands of south-central Africa. As an obligate subterranean forager, it exhibits several physiological traits attuned to the hypoxic, thermally stable environment of sealed burrow systems. Basal oxygen consumption, measured via open-flow respirometry at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], averages 58.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 58.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the reduced metabolic rates documented in other subterranean mammals. This diminished resting metabolism likely reflects energetic savings from a sedentary lifestyle and the low partial pressure of oxygen within deep tunnel networks. The typical gestation period at a thermoneutral temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] is 58 days [tg = 58 days], though a range extending from 56 to 61 days has been observed in captive colonies. Such a relatively lengthy developmental interval for a rodent of this size may be linked to the altricial state of the neonates, which require substantial in utero maturation before parturition.

Neonatal body mass in the Mashona mole-rat is remarkably modest, with newborn individuals weighing approximately 8 grams [Wwb = approximately 8 grams], a value estimated from measurements reported for the closely related Cryptomys hottentotus, for which direct data on Fukomys darlingi remain scarce. This low birth mass classifies the pups as altricial, requiring extended maternal investment during a prolonged period of lactation. Under stable thermal conditions at an ambient temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], weaning—defined as the cessation of milk ingestion and the onset of nutritional independence—occurs 82 days since birth [tx = 82 days since birth], a milestone extrapolated from developmental timelines in Cryptomys hottentotus. The extended weaning phase is notable among bathyergids and highlights a reproductive strategy that prioritises intense care of a small number of offspring over rapid turnover. Female reproductive output reflects this strategy, with litters typically comprising from 1 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 7 pups per litter], and females producing between 2 and 3 litters per year [F_R_i = between 2 and 3 litters per year].

Sexual maturation proceeds gradually in this social rodent, with individuals reaching puberty at an estimated 450 days since birth [tp = 450 days since birth], as inferred from growth and reproductive data for Cryptomys hottentotus at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The onset of gonadal activity occurs long after weaning, suggesting a considerable period of somatic growth and social integration within the natal colony before reproductive competence is attained. Adult body size in Fukomys darlingi exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism: females attain a maximum wet body mass of 92 grams [Wwi = 92 grams], with reported values ranging between 54 and 92 grams, whereas males reach an ultimate weight of 80 grams [Wwi = 80 grams], spanning a range of 60 to 80 grams. This pattern, with females exceeding males in mass, is characteristic of several cooperatively breeding bathyergids and may be linked to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation incurred by the dominant breeding female. The substantial investment in offspring, from the prolonged gestation of 58 days to the lengthy lactation period, necessitates a stable colony structure that facilitates cooperative care and resource provisioning.

Longevity in the Mashona mole-rat is exceptionally high for a rodent of its body size, with a maximum recorded lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years], a figure approximated from field and captive records of the congeneric Cryptomys hottentotus at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, typical of subterranean rodents that inhabit predator-buffered, stable environments, is associated with a slow life-history pace characterised by delayed puberty, a modest annual reproductive rate, and intensive postnatal care. Such a life-history strategy, coupled with the high degree of reproductive skew within colonies, where reproduction is often monopolised by a single breeding pair, underscores the adaptive value of sociality in this species. The maximum reproductive rate observed under optimal captive conditions, maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], reflects the combined probability of 2 to 3 litters being produced per year in the dominant female.

Comparative life-history analyses among African mole-rats reveal that Mashona mole-rats occupy an intermediate position along a continuum of social complexity and reproductive investment. Unlike the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber), which exhibits extreme reproductive skew and exceptionally long lifespans exceeding 30 years, Fukomys darlingi presents a more moderate but still markedly slow life-history syndrome. With a duration of 58 days [tg = 58 days], spanning from 56 to 61 days, the gestation in this species is relatively short, and small litter sizes of 1 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 7 pups per litter] place it closer to solitary bathyergids in reproductive output than to the naked mole-rat at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. However, the extended weaning period of 82 days since birth [tx = 82 days since birth] under stable thermoneutral conditions (37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]) and the delayed onset of puberty at 450 days since birth [tp = 450 days since birth] align more closely with social species. Colony dynamics, including the suppression of reproduction in non-breeding females and the cooperative rearing of offspring, further reinforce the ecological and evolutionary connections between sociality and slow life histories in this fascinating lineage.
